title: First-time PC builder: where should the money go?
keywords: where to spend money on pc
new to building pc what to buy first

question_tree.question: What will you mainly use the PC for?

next.text:
1. Spend the biggest share (roughly 35 to 40 percent of your budget) on the graphics card, since it decides how smooth games look.
2. Spend about 15 to 20 percent on the processor, and about 10 percent each on the motherboard, RAM and storage.
3. Spend about 8 to 10 percent on a good power supply — it protects every other part, so don't pick the cheapest one.
4. Leave a little room for a decent case with airflow.

1. Prioritise the processor, RAM (16GB or more) and a fast SSD. These three decide how fast the PC feels day to day.
2. You usually don't need a separate graphics card unless your work needs one.
3. Don't skip the power supply quality; pick a reliable brand even on a tight budget.

1. Decide your main use first. It decides where the money should go, and every other choice follows from it.
2. A safe default for any build: a good power supply, an SSD instead of a hard drive, and at least 16GB of RAM.
3. Buy parts only from sellers who give a proper GST bill, since you need it for warranty claims later.

title: Should I buy a prebuilt PC or build my own?
keywords: should i build my own pc

question_tree.question: How comfortable are you with assembling a PC?

options.answer: Comfortable — I've done it or I'm happy to follow a guide

next.text:
1. Building yourself usually gives the best value, because you pay for parts and not for a brand's markup, and you pick every part.
2. Make a parts list first and check that everything is compatible (socket, RAM type, case size, power).
3. Buy from reliable sellers and keep all bills for warranty.

options.answer: No, but I'm willing to learn

next.text:
1. Watch a couple of full beginner build videos for your type of parts before buying anything.
2. Alternatively, buy the parts yourself and ask a local shop to assemble them for a small fee — you still get the savings and an expert does the tricky part.
3. Keep the bills for every part, as each part has its own warranty.

options.answer: No, I want something ready to use

next.text:
1. A branded prebuilt PC or a local assembled PC are both fine options. Ask a local assembler for an itemised quote that lists every part, so you can see exactly what you're paying for.
2. Check that the warranty is clearly written and covers each part, not just the whole PC.
3. Be careful of deals that hide a weak power supply or very little RAM — those are the most common shortcuts.
